diagnostics.notes: *   **Clinical Diagnosis:** Diagnosis is made based on history and physical exam findings alone. *   **No laboratory or imaging studies** are required for an isolated, uncomplicated superficial burn. *   Assessment of **Total Body Surface Area (TBSA)** can be done using the "Rule of Nines" (for adults) or the Lund-Browder chart (for children), but it is primarily used for guiding fluid resuscitation in deeper, more extensive burns. It is still good practice to document the approximate TBSA involved.

DERM__burns__superficial_firstdegree_bur.overview: A superficial burn, also known as a first-degree burn, is the least severe type of burn, involving injury confined to the **outermost layer of the skin, the epidermis**. It is characterized by erythema (redness), pain, and dryness, but does not produce blisters. These burns typically heal within 3-7 days without scarring. The classic example is a mild sunburn.
DERM__burns__superficial_firstdegree_bur.etiologyPathophysiology: **Etiology:** *   **Thermal:** Most common cause. Brief exposure to hot liquids (scalds), hot surfaces, or flash flames. *   **Radiation:** Overexposure to ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun (sunburn) or tanning beds. Also seen with radiation therapy for cancer. *   **Chemical:** Brief exposure to mild irritants or acids. *   **Electrical:** Rarely causes an isolated superficial burn; usually associated with more significant deeper injury.  **Pathophysiology:** 1.  Tissue injury to the epidermis triggers an acute inflammatory response. 2.  Release of inflammatory mediators (e.g., prostaglandins, histamine, kinins) from damaged keratinocytes. 3.  These mediators cause local vasodilation and increased capillary permeability. 4.  Vasodilation leads to **erythema** (redness) and warmth. 5.  Mild leakage of plasma into the interstitium causes minor edema, but not enough to separate the epidermis from the dermis to form blisters. 6.  Prostaglandins and other mediators sensitize local nociceptors (pain receptors), resulting in **pain and tenderness**. 7.  The damaged epidermis typically desquamates (peels) in several days as new epithelial cells regenerate from the basal layer.
DERM__burns__superficial_firstdegree_bur.epidemiology: *   Extremely common; one of the most frequent types of injuries seen in outpatient and emergency settings. *   Occurs in all age groups. *   Children and the elderly are particularly susceptible to scald injuries. *   Sunburn is a major cause, especially in individuals with lighter skin phototypes (Fitzpatrick I-II) and during summer months.
DERM__burns__superficial_firstdegree_bur.clinicalPresentation: *   A patient presents with a history of recent exposure to a noxious source (e.g., "I was out in the sun all day," "I spilled hot coffee on my arm"). *   The onset of pain and redness is typically within a few hours of the injury. *   The primary complaint is pain, which can be significant despite the superficial nature of the injury.
DERM__burns__superficial_firstdegree_bur.prognosis: *   **Excellent.** *   Healing typically occurs within **3 to 7 days**. *   There is **no scarring**, although temporary pigment changes may occur.
riskFactors: Extremes of age (infants, elderly) due to thinner skin and delayed reaction times.
Occupational exposure (e.g., chefs, welders, firefighters).
Fair skin phototypes (Fitzpatrick I-II) for UV-induced burns.
Use of photosensitizing medications (e.g., tetracyclines, thiazides, retinoids).
Impaired mobility or cognitive function.
Peripheral neuropathy (e.g., diabetic neuropathy), leading to decreased sensation.
Lack of home safety measures (e.g., water heater set >120F/49C, no smoke detectors).
symptoms: Pain and tenderness in the affected area.
Erythema (redness of the skin).
Sensation of warmth or heat.
Pruritus (itching), particularly during the healing phase.
examFindings: Erythematous skin that blanches with pressure.
Dry surface with no blistering, vesicles, or bullae.
Absence of weeping or exudate.
Epidermis is intact.
Possible mild edema.
Area is tender to palpation.
Brisk capillary refill.
treatment: Immediate cooling: Apply cool running water or compresses for 10-20 minutes. Avoid ice, as it can cause vasoconstriction and further tissue damage.
Analgesia: Oral NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen) are preferred for their anti-prostaglandin effect. Acetaminophen can also be used.
Topical care: Application of soothing, bland emollients or moisturizers (e.g., aloe vera gel, petrolatum-based ointments) to relieve pain and prevent drying.
Hydration: Encourage adequate oral fluid intake, especially for extensive burns like sunburn.
Tetanus prophylaxis is not indicated as the skin barrier remains intact.
management: Patient Education: Counsel on sun protection (sunscreen, protective clothing), and home safety measures to prevent recurrence.
Symptom Control: Continue oral analgesics and topical moisturizers as needed.
Monitoring: Instruct patient to monitor for signs of deeper injury or infection (rare), such as blister formation, purulent drainage, or fever.
Follow-up: Routine follow-up is typically not necessary for uncomplicated superficial burns.
Skin Care: Advise patient to avoid peeling the skin (desquamation) and to protect the area from sun exposure to minimize pigmentary changes.
complications: Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation or hypopigmentation: Altered skin color in the affected area after healing.
Desquamation: Peeling of the superficial epidermis, which is a normal part of healing but may be cosmetically undesirable.
Pain and discomfort: May temporarily limit function or sleep.
Dehydration: A rare complication seen only in cases of very extensive total body surface area (TBSA) involvement (e.g., severe sunburn).
Infection: Extremely uncommon as the epidermal barrier is not breached.

diagnostics.notes: Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on history and physical exam. The main diagnostic tasks are to determine the **depth** of the burn and the **Total Body Surface Area (TBSA)** involved. *   **TBSA Estimation:** *   **Rule of Nines (Adults):** A rapid estimation method. *   Head: 9% *   Each Arm: 9% *   Anterior Torso: 18% *   Posterior Torso: 18% *   Each Leg: 18% *   Genitalia/Perineum: 1% *   **Lund-Browder Chart:** More accurate, especially for pediatric patients, as it accounts for changes in body proportions with age. *   **Palmar Method:** The surface of the patient's palm (including fingers) represents ~1% TBSA. Useful for small or scattered burns. *   **Laboratory Studies (for major burns >20% TBSA or suspected systemic effects):** *   **CBC:** To assess for hemoconcentration (elevated Hct) from fluid loss. *   **CMP:** To monitor electrolytes (hyperkalemia initially), BUN/Cr (renal function), and albumin (protein loss). *   **CK-MB / Troponin:** If electrical injury is suspected, to rule out cardiac muscle damage. *   **Urinalysis:** To check for myoglobinuria (rhabdomyolysis) in deep or electrical burns. *   **ABG with Carboxyhemoglobin:** Essential if inhalation injury is suspected.

DERM__burns__partialthickness_seconddegr.overview: A partial-thickness burn, also known as a second-degree burn, is an injury that damages the epidermis and extends into the dermis. This category is further subdivided into **superficial partial-thickness** and **deep partial-thickness** burns, which differ in their depth, clinical appearance, and prognosis. The key feature distinguishing them from first-degree burns is the presence of blistering and damage to the dermal layer.
DERM__burns__partialthickness_seconddegr.etiologyPathophysiology: **Etiology:** *   **Thermal (most common):** *   **Scalds:** Hot liquids or steam (common in children). *   **Flame:** Direct contact with fire. *   **Contact:** Touching a hot object (e.g., stove, iron). *   **Flash:** Intense heat from an explosion. *   **Chemical:** Contact with strong acids or alkalis. *   **Electrical:** Passage of electrical current through tissue. *   **Radiation:** Severe sunburn or exposure to radiation sources.  **Pathophysiology:** *   Tissue damage extends from the epidermis into the dermis, damaging blood vessels, nerve endings, and dermal appendages (hair follicles, sweat glands). *   An intense inflammatory response is triggered, causing significant vasodilation and a dramatic increase in capillary permeability. *   This increased permeability allows protein-rich plasma to leak from the intravascular space into the interstitium, leading to edema and the formation of **blisters (bullae)**. *   **Superficial Partial-Thickness:** Damage is limited to the epidermis and the papillary (upper) dermis. Nerve endings are irritated and exposed, causing significant pain. The vascular network is largely intact, leading to brisk blanching. *   **Deep Partial-Thickness:** Damage extends into the deeper reticular dermis. More nerve endings are destroyed, which can result in less pain compared to superficial burns. Blood vessels are more damaged, leading to sluggish or absent blanching. Glandular tissue and hair follicles are often damaged.
DERM__burns__partialthickness_seconddegr.epidemiology: *   Burns are a major cause of morbidity worldwide. *   In the U.S., approximately 486,000 people receive medical treatment for burns annually. *   **Scald burns** are the most common type in children under 5 years old. *   Flame burns are more common in older children and adults. *   Most burns occur in the home.
DERM__burns__partialthickness_seconddegr.clinicalPresentation: The patient's history is critical. A detailed account of the incident helps determine the burn agent, duration of contact, and potential for associated injuries (e.g., inhalation injury in a house fire, trauma from an explosion). The patient will present with an acutely painful, blistered, and edematous area of skin following a known exposure.
DERM__burns__partialthickness_seconddegr.prognosis: *   **Superficial Partial-Thickness:** Excellent prognosis. Typically heals within 2-3 weeks via re-epithelialization. Scarring is minimal, though pigment changes are common. *   **Deep Partial-Thickness:** Healing takes longer (3-8 weeks) and often occurs by scar formation rather than re-epithelialization. There is a high risk of significant hypertrophic scarring and contractures. Skin grafting may be required for optimal functional and cosmetic outcomes.
riskFactors: Extremes of age (infants, young children, and elderly) due to thinner skin and altered response capabilities.
Occupational exposures (e.g., firefighters, chefs, industrial workers).
Underlying medical conditions such as peripheral neuropathy (e.g., diabetes mellitus), seizure disorders, or impaired mobility.
Substance abuse or altered mental status.
Unsafe living conditions (e.g., lack of smoke detectors, faulty wiring, use of open flames for heating).
Child abuse, elder abuse, or self-inflicted injury.
symptoms: Severe pain (especially in superficial partial-thickness burns due to exposed nerve endings).
Blister (bulla) formation, which may be intact or ruptured.
Moist, weeping, or exudative skin surface.
Localized edema (swelling).
Erythema (redness) of the affected and surrounding skin.
examFindings: **Superficial Partial-Thickness Burn:**
- Appearance: Moist, pink or red, weeping surface.
- Blisters: Prominent, thin-walled, and filled with serous fluid.
- Capillary Refill: Brisk; the area blanches with pressure and color returns quickly.
- Sensation: Extremely painful and hypersensitive to touch and air.
**Deep Partial-Thickness Burn:**
- Appearance: Mottled, with areas of cherry red, waxy white, or pale coloration. Can be wet or dry.
- Blisters: Often ruptured or thick-walled; underlying tissue is less pink.
- Capillary Refill: Sluggish or absent; blanching is slow or does not occur.
- Sensation: Diminished sensation to pinprick or light touch due to nerve damage; may be less painful than superficial burns.
treatment: **Initial/Pre-hospital Care:**
- Stop the burning process: Remove hot/smoldering clothing and cool the burn with cool (not ice-cold) running water for up to 20 minutes.
- Cover the wound with a clean, dry dressing or sheet.
- Assess ABCs (Airway, Breathing, Circulation), with special attention to signs of inhalation injury (hoarseness, soot in nares, stridor).
**Emergency Department & Inpatient Care:**

- **Fluid Resuscitation (for >15-20% TBSA):** Utilize the Parkland formula (4 mL Lactated Ringer's x kg body weight x %TBSA burn) to guide IV fluid administration. Give half over the first 8 hours post-injury and the remaining half over the next 16 hours. Titrate to maintain urine output of 0.5-1.0 mL/kg/hr.
- **Wound Care:**
- Gentle cleansing with sterile water or chlorhexidine.
- Debridement of ruptured blisters and non-viable tissue. Management of intact blisters is controversial; they may be left intact or debrided.
- Application of topical antimicrobial agents (e.g., silver sulfadiazine, bacitracin, mafenide acetate) to prevent infection.
- Application of non-adherent, absorbent dressings.
- **Pain Management:** Aggressive analgesia, typically with parenteral opioids (e.g., morphine, fentanyl), especially for dressing changes. NSAIDs may be used as adjuncts.
- **Tetanus Prophylaxis:** Administer tetanus toxoid based on immunization history.
- **Surgical Intervention:** Deep partial-thickness burns that fail to heal within 2-3 weeks may require excision and skin grafting.
management: **Burn Center Referral:** Consider for burns >10% TBSA, burns involving hands, face, feet, genitalia, or major joints, circumferential burns, and high-voltage electrical or significant chemical burns.

**Rehabilitation:** Early initiation of physical and occupational therapy is critical to preserve range of motion and prevent joint contractures. Splinting may be required to maintain functional position.
**Scar Management:**
- Use of pressure garments and silicone gel sheeting to minimize hypertrophic scarring.
- Scar massage and moisturization to improve pliability.

**Nutritional Support:** Provide a high-protein, high-calorie diet to counteract the hypermetabolic state induced by the burn and support wound healing. Enteral or parenteral nutrition may be necessary for large burns.
**Psychosocial Support:** Address potential for PTSD, anxiety, depression, and body image disturbance through counseling and support groups.
complications: **Infection:** Progression from local wound infection to cellulitis or invasive sepsis is a major cause of morbidity and mortality.
**Hypovolemic Shock (Burn Shock):** Occurs early due to massive fluid shifts from the intravascular to the interstitial space.
**Compartment Syndrome:** In circumferential limb burns, swelling can compromise vascular and nerve function, requiring emergent escharotomy.
**Hypertrophic Scarring and Keloids:** Abnormal, raised scar formation that can be pruritic and painful.
**Contractures:** Tightening of scar tissue across joints, leading to significant loss of function and deformity.
**Rhabdomyolysis and Acute Kidney Injury (AKI):** Particularly with deep or extensive burns.
**Dyspigmentation:** Permanent changes in skin color (hyper- or hypopigmentation) in the healed area.
**Marjolin's Ulcer:** A rare, late complication involving the development of squamous cell carcinoma in a chronic burn scar.

diagnostics.notes: *   **Lab Studies:** *   **CBC:** Initially shows high hematocrit (hemoconcentration) from fluid loss. *   **CMP:** Monitor for electrolyte abnormalities (hyperkalemia initially from cell lysis, then hypokalemia), renal function (BUN/Cr), and albumin (hypoalbuminemia). *   **CK (Creatine Kinase):** Markedly elevated in electrical burns or deep burns with muscle damage, indicating rhabdomyolysis. *   **ABG with Carboxyhemoglobin (CO-Hgb):** Essential if inhalation injury or carbon monoxide poisoning is suspected. *   **Lactate:** To assess for shock and adequacy of resuscitation. *   **Urinalysis:** Check for myoglobinuria (dark, tea-colored urine) in rhabdomyolysis. *   **Imaging:** *   **Chest X-ray:** To evaluate for inhalation injury (may show ARDS, but is often normal initially). *   **Bronchoscopy:** Gold standard for diagnosing the level and severity of airway injury.

DERM__burns__fullthickness_thirdfourthde.overview: A full-thickness burn is a severe injury that destroys all layers of the skin, including the epidermis and the entire dermis, and extends into the subcutaneous fat. These are classified as **third-degree** burns. When the injury extends deeper, damaging underlying muscle, tendon, and bone, it is classified as a **fourth-degree** burn. Due to the complete destruction of dermal nerve endings, the central area of the burn is insensate. Full-thickness burns do not heal by re-epithelialization and require surgical intervention (skin grafting) for closure. They are associated with significant systemic complications, including burn shock, and carry a high risk of morbidity and mortality.
DERM__burns__fullthickness_thirdfourthde.epidemiology: *   Bimodal age distribution: peaks in children <5 years old (scalds are common) and young adults 18-35 years old (flame burns). A third peak occurs in the elderly. *   Flame burns are the most common cause of burn-related deaths. *   Most burns occur in the home.
DERM__burns__fullthickness_thirdfourthde.clinicalPresentation: The patient presents following a significant thermal, chemical, or electrical injury. The primary focus is the **ABCDEs** (Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure). Suspect **inhalation injury** if the burn occurred in an enclosed space, or if there is facial/neck swelling, hoarseness, carbonaceous sputum, or singed nasal hairs. The patient may be in hypovolemic shock with hypotension and tachycardia. The burn wound itself will be the most obvious finding on exposure.
DERM__burns__fullthickness_thirdfourthde.prognosis: Prognosis depends heavily on: 1.  **TBSA burned** 2.  **Patient age** (very young and very old have worse outcomes) 3.  **Presence of inhalation injury** (significantly increases mortality) *   **Baux Score:** A classic predictor of mortality, calculated as **Patient Age + % TBSA**. A score >140 is generally considered non-survivable.
DERM__burns__fullthickness_thirdfourthde.etiologyPathophysiology: Full-thickness burns result from the complete destruction of the epidermis and dermis, extending into subcutaneous tissue (third-degree) and potentially underlying muscle, tendon, and bone (fourth-degree). Common etiologies include thermal injuries (flame, scald, contact), high-voltage electrical currents, and potent chemical agents (e.g., strong alkalis causing liquefactive necrosis or acids causing coagulation necrosis). The pathophysiology is characterized by three zones of injury. The central zone of coagulation is an area of irreversible necrosis. Surrounding this is the zone of stasis, where tissue is ischemic and potentially salvageable with adequate resuscitation. The outermost zone of hyperemia is characterized by vasodilation and will recover. Systemically, a massive inflammatory response triggers a surge in cytokines, leading to increased capillary permeability. This causes a profound fluid shift from the intravascular to the interstitial space, resulting in burn shock-a combination of distributive and hypovolemic shock. This state is marked by hemoconcentration, decreased cardiac output, and end-organ hypoperfusion. The body enters a severe hypermetabolic and hypercatabolic state. Destruction of muscle in deep burns leads to rhabdomyolysis, releasing myoglobin and potassium, which can precipitate acute kidney injury and cardiac arrhythmias.
riskFactors: Age extremes (infants and elderly) due to thinner skin and reduced physiologic reserve
Occupational exposures (e.g., firefighters, electricians, chemical plant workers)
Underlying medical conditions, such as diabetes mellitus, peripheral neuropathy, or peripheral vascular disease
Altered mental status from substance use, psychiatric conditions, or neurologic disorders (e.g., seizures)
Unsafe housing conditions (e.g., no smoke detectors, faulty wiring)
Assault, abuse, or self-immolation
symptoms: Insensate or painless central burn area due to destruction of dermal nerve endings
Surrounding areas of partial-thickness burn may be extremely painful
Visible charred, white, or leathery appearance of the skin
In cases of inhalation injury: hoarseness, cough, stridor, shortness of breath, or carbonaceous sputum
examFindings: Skin appears leathery, waxy, white, or charred black (eschar)
The surface is dry, firm, and non-blanching
Painless to pinprick or light touch in the central area
Visible thrombosed subcutaneous veins
Hairs are easily epilated (pull out without resistance)
In fourth-degree burns, there is visible exposure of subcutaneous fat, muscle, tendon, or bone

Circumferential burns may present with signs of compartment syndrome (6 P's: Pain, Pallor, Paresthesias, Pulselessness, Poikilothermia, Paralysis) in an extremity or compromised ventilation if on the torso
Systemic signs of shock (tachycardia, hypotension, oliguria)
treatment: **Pre-hospital/Acute:** Stop the burning process, ensure ABCs (Airway with early intubation for suspected inhalation injury, Breathing, Circulation), administer 100% O2, and begin fluid resuscitation with Lactated Ringer's via two large-bore IVs.

**Fluid Resuscitation:** Guided by the Parkland formula (4 mL/kg/%TBSA), administering half over the first 8 hours from injury and the remainder over the next 16 hours. Titrate to maintain urine output of 0.5-1.0 mL/kg/hr in adults.
**Wound Care:** Cleanse the wound, debride loose tissue, and apply topical antimicrobial agents (e.g., silver sulfadiazine, mafenide acetate). Provide tetanus prophylaxis.
**Pain Management:** Administer IV opioids (e.g., morphine, fentanyl) for procedural pain and pain from associated partial-thickness burns.
**Surgical Intervention:**

*   **Escharotomy/Fasciotomy:** Emergent surgical incisions through the eschar (escharotomy) and/or fascia (fasciotomy) to relieve pressure and restore circulation in circumferential burns causing compartment syndrome.

*   **Excision and Grafting:** The definitive treatment. Early surgical excision of all necrotic tissue followed by coverage with split-thickness autografts. Temporary coverage may be achieved with allografts or synthetic skin substitutes.
**Nutritional Support:** Initiate early enteral nutrition to support the hypermetabolic state and prevent catabolism.
management: **Rehabilitation:** Intensive physical and occupational therapy is critical to prevent joint contractures, maintain range of motion, and maximize functional recovery. Splinting of affected joints in a functional position is often required.
**Scar Management:** Use of compression garments (worn 23 hours/day for 12-18 months) and silicone gel sheets to minimize hypertrophic scarring and improve scar pliability.
**Pruritus Control:** Management of severe post-burn itching with antihistamines, topical moisturizers, and gabapentin.
**Psychosocial Support:** Long-term counseling and support groups to address PTSD, depression, anxiety, and body image issues.
**Surgical Reconstruction:** Staged reconstructive procedures may be necessary to release contractures, improve cosmetic appearance, and restore function.
complications: **Systemic:** Burn shock, ARDS (from inhalation injury or SIRS), sepsis (leading cause of late mortality), acute kidney injury (from myoglobinuria or hypoperfusion), hypothermia, Curling's ulcer (GI stress ulcer), and venous thromboembolism.
**Local/Wound:** Burn wound infection, cellulitis, compartment syndrome in circumferential burns.

**Long-term:** Hypertrophic scarring, keloids, severe joint contractures leading to functional disability, chronic pain, peripheral neuropathy, severe pruritus, and psychological sequelae (PTSD, depression).
**Malignancy:** Marjolin's ulcer, a rare but aggressive squamous cell carcinoma, can develop in chronic, non-healing burn wounds or old burn scars decades after the initial injury.

diagnostics.notes: *   **Labs:** *   **CBC:** **Elevated Hct (hemoconcentration)** is a classic initial finding. *   **CMP:** *   **Hyperkalemia** (early, from cell lysis). *   **Hyponatremia** (from fluid shifts). *   BUN/Creatinine (to assess for AKI). *   Glucose (hyperglycemia from stress response). *   **ABG with Carboxyhemoglobin (COHb):** Assess for metabolic acidosis (from hypoperfusion) and carbon monoxide poisoning. Standard pulse oximetry is unreliable in CO poisoning. *   **CK (Creatine Kinase) & Urine Myoglobin:** Essential for electrical burns or suspected rhabdomyolysis. *   **Type and Screen:** In case of associated trauma or need for future surgery. *   **Lactate:** Key marker of systemic hypoperfusion. *   **Imaging:** *   **Chest X-ray:** May be normal initially. Used to rule out associated trauma and establish a baseline. Later may show infiltrates or ARDS. *   **EKG:** Mandatory for all electrical burns and patients with cardiac history.

DERM__burns__burn_shock__fluid_resuscita.overview: Burn shock is a complex, life-threatening condition that occurs after a major burn injury (typically >20% Total Body Surface Area). It is a combination of **distributive shock** (due to systemic inflammation and vasodilation) and **hypovolemic shock** (due to massive fluid loss from the intravascular space). The underlying pathophysiology is a systemic inflammatory response leading to a profound increase in capillary permeability, causing fluid to shift into the interstitial space. Prompt and aggressive fluid resuscitation is the cornerstone of management to prevent end-organ hypoperfusion and failure.
DERM__burns__burn_shock__fluid_resuscita.etiologyPathophysiology: The pathophysiology of burn shock is a two-phase process involving both a local and a systemic response.  **Local Response (Jackson's Burn Model):** *   **Zone of Coagulation:** Central area of the burn with the most intense heat. Cells are irreversibly damaged and necrosed. *   **Zone of Stasis:** Surrounds the central zone. Characterized by decreased tissue perfusion. This tissue is potentially salvageable with adequate resuscitation but can progress to necrosis without it. *   **Zone of Hyperemia:** Outermost zone. Tissue perfusion is increased due to vasodilation. This tissue will typically recover unless severe sepsis or prolonged hypoperfusion occurs.  **Systemic Response (The "Leaky Capillaries"):** 1.  **Massive Inflammatory Mediator Release:** A major burn triggers a Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS). Damaged tissue releases a "cytokine storm" including histamine, prostaglandins, leukotrienes, TNF-alpha, and interleukins. 2.  **Increased Capillary Permeability:** These mediators cause a dramatic increase in microvascular permeability, not just at the burn site but **systemically**. 3.  **Intravascular Fluid Loss:** Plasma, electrolytes, and proteins (especially albumin) leak from the intravascular space into the interstitial space. This leads to: *   **Profound Intravascular Hypovolemia:** Leads to decreased cardiac preload, decreased cardiac output, and systemic hypoperfusion (shock). *   **Massive Edema:** Both at the burn site and in non-burned tissues. 4.  **Cardiovascular Effects:** *   **Initial Phase (Ebb Phase):** Decreased cardiac output and increased systemic vascular resistance (SVR) due to hypovolemia and catecholamine release. Myocardial depressant factors are also released. *   **Later Phase (Flow Phase):** After resuscitation, a hypermetabolic state with increased cardiac output and decreased SVR develops. 5.  **Hemoconcentration:** Loss of plasma volume from the vascular space leads to an increased hematocrit.
DERM__burns__burn_shock__fluid_resuscita.epidemiology: *   **Incidence:** Approximately 486,000 burn injuries receive medical treatment annually in the US. *   **Etiology:** *   Flame/Fire: ~43% *   Scalds (hot liquid/steam): ~34% *   Direct contact with hot object: ~9% *   Electrical: ~4% *   Chemical: ~3% *   **Mortality:** The risk of death increases significantly with larger burn size (%TBSA), advanced age, and the presence of inhalation injury.
DERM__burns__burn_shock__fluid_resuscita.clinicalPresentation: A patient with a significant burn presents with evidence of thermal injury and progressive signs of shock. The presentation evolves over the first 24-48 hours. Initially, blood pressure may be normal due to compensatory vasoconstriction, but tachycardia is almost always present. As fluid shifts continue without resuscitation, signs of hypoperfusion become evident. Massive edema is a hallmark finding that develops over hours.
DERM__burns__burn_shock__fluid_resuscita.prognosis: Prognosis depends heavily on three key factors: 1.  **% TBSA burned** 2.  **Patient Age** 3.  **Presence of Inhalation Injury**  *   **Baux Score:** A simple prognostic indicator = **Patient Age + %TBSA**. A score > 140 is associated with very high mortality. The presence of inhalation injury adds ~20% mortality to any given burn size.
riskFactors: Burn size >20% Total Body Surface Area (TBSA)
Extremes of age (pediatric <2 years, adults >60 years)
Presence of full-thickness burns
Concomitant inhalational injury
Associated traumatic injuries
Pre-existing comorbidities (cardiac, renal, hepatic disease, diabetes)
Delayed initiation of resuscitation (>2 hours post-injury)
Electrical burns (often cause extensive deep tissue damage)
symptoms: Profound thirst
Altered mental status (anxiety, confusion, lethargy)
Oliguria or anuria
Nausea and vomiting (secondary to paralytic ileus)
Dyspnea (if associated with inhalational injury or developing ARDS)
Feeling cold or shivering
examFindings: **Vitals:** Tachycardia (early), hypotension (late, ominous sign), tachypnea, hypothermia.
**Cardiovascular:** Delayed capillary refill (>3 seconds), weak or thready peripheral pulses, cool extremities.
**Renal:** Oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/hr in adults) or anuria.
**Neurologic:** Decreased level of consciousness, confusion, or agitation.
**GI:** Hypoactive or absent bowel sounds, abdominal distension.
**Integumentary:** Presence of burn injury, massive generalized edema (anasarca) affecting both burned and unburned tissue.
**Pulmonary (if inhalational injury):** Stridor, hoarseness, wheezing, carbonaceous sputum, facial burns.
treatment: **1. Initial Access and Fluid Choice:**
- Establish two large-bore (16 gauge) peripheral IVs, preferably through unburned skin. If unavailable, use intraosseous (IO) or central venous access.
- Fluid of choice: **Lactated Ringer's (LR)** is preferred over Normal Saline to avoid hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis.
**2. Fluid Resuscitation Formulas (as a starting guide):**
- **Parkland Formula (most common):** Total fluid in 24 hrs = **4 mL LR x Body Weight (kg) x %TBSA**.
- Administer the first half over the first 8 hours **from the time of injury**.
- Administer the second half over the subsequent 16 hours.
- **Modified Brooke Formula:** 2 mL LR x Body Weight (kg) x %TBSA. Same administration timing.
**3. Titration to Clinical Endpoints (Critical Step):**
- Formulas are an estimate; fluid administration must be titrated based on patient response.
- **Primary Goal:** Urine Output (UOP) via Foley catheter.
- Adults: Maintain 0.5 - 1.0 mL/kg/hr.
- Children (<30 kg): Maintain 1.0 mL/kg/hr.
- Electrical burns/rhabdomyolysis: Target higher UOP (1-2 mL/kg/hr) to clear myoglobin.
- **Secondary Goals:**
- Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) > 65 mmHg.
- Heart Rate < 120 bpm.
- Normalizing serum lactate and base deficit.
- Clear sensorium.
**4. Adjunctive Therapies:**
- **Colloids (Albumin):** Generally avoided in the first 12-24 hours due to capillary leak. May be considered after this period to reduce total fluid requirements ('rescue' therapy).
- **Vasopressors:** Used as a last resort for refractory shock unresponsive to adequate volume resuscitation, as they can worsen peripheral ischemia.
management: **Monitoring:**
- Strict hourly intake and output monitoring.
- Continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring.
- Frequent assessment of peripheral perfusion (pulses, capillary refill).
- Serial laboratory evaluation (ABG, lactate, electrolytes, CK).
- Invasive monitoring (arterial line) for hemodynamically unstable patients.
**Complication Prevention:**
- **Avoiding "Fluid Creep" (Over-resuscitation):** Meticulously titrate fluids to the minimum necessary to achieve endpoints to prevent compartment syndromes and ARDS.
- **Compartment Syndrome Surveillance:**
- **Abdominal:** Monitor for increasing abdominal distension and high peak inspiratory pressures. Measure bladder pressures serially (IAP > 20 mmHg is concerning for ACS).
- **Extremity:** Perform frequent neurovascular checks of circumferentially burned limbs; be prepared for escharotomy or fasciotomy.
**Supportive Care:**
- Early enteral nutrition to maintain gut integrity.
- Aggressive pain and anxiety management.
- Temperature regulation (warming blankets) to prevent hypothermia.
- DVT and stress ulcer prophylaxis.
complications: **Complications of Under-Resuscitation:**
- Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) from acute tubular necrosis (ATN).
- Conversion of burns from partial- to full-thickness (extension of the zone of stasis).
- Mesenteric ischemia and paralytic ileus.
- Multi-organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS) and death.
**Complications of Over-Resuscitation ("Fluid Creep"):**
- **Abdominal Compartment Syndrome (ACS):** A life-threatening emergency caused by massive visceral edema, requiring decompressive laparotomy.
- **Extremity Compartment Syndrome:** Requires emergent escharotomy/fasciotomy.
- Pulmonary Edema and Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS).
- Cerebral edema.
**Metabolic Complications:**
- Persistent metabolic acidosis.
- Severe electrolyte derangements (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia initially, then hypokalemia).
- Hypothermia due to large volumes of room-temperature fluids and loss of skin barrier.

diagnostics.notes: *   The diagnosis is **primarily clinical**, based on history and characteristic physical exam findings. *   **Dermoscopy** can aid in visualization, showing a "strawberry pattern" (erythematous pseudo-network around hair follicles). *   **Skin Biopsy (Shave or Punch)** is indicated if there is suspicion for SCC. "Red flags" for progression include: *   **Induration** (firmness at the base) *   **Ulceration** or bleeding *   **Rapid growth** *   **Tenderness/Pain** *   Diameter > 1 cm *   Failure to respond to appropriate therapy ---

DERM__malignancy__actinic_keratosis.overview: Actinic Keratosis (AK), also known as solar keratosis, is a common, pre-malignant lesion of the epidermis caused by chronic, cumulative exposure to ultraviolet (UV) radiation. It is considered a precursor lesion to squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), specifically SCC in situ or invasive SCC. AKs represent atypical keratinocytes confined to the epidermis. They are a significant marker for chronically sun-damaged skin and an increased risk for all forms of skin cancer.  ---
DERM__malignancy__actinic_keratosis.etiologyPathophysiology: *   **Etiology**: The primary cause is long-term exposure to **ultraviolet (UV) radiation**, primarily UVB (290-320 nm) and to a lesser extent UVA (320-400 nm). *   **Pathophysiology**: 1.  UV radiation induces DNA damage in epidermal keratinocytes. 2.  The most common mutation occurs in the **TP53 tumor suppressor gene**, leading to impaired apoptosis (programmed cell death) of damaged cells. 3.  This allows for the clonal proliferation and survival of atypical keratinocytes. 4.  These atypical cells are confined to the epidermis and **do not breach the basement membrane**. If they do, the lesion has progressed to invasive SCC. 5.  The concept of **"field cancerization"** describes a large area of sun-damaged skin (e.g., the entire scalp) containing multiple clinical and subclinical AKs, all at risk for malignant transformation.  ---
DERM__malignancy__actinic_keratosis.epidemiology: *   One of the most common dermatologic diagnoses, especially in older adults. *   Prevalence increases significantly with age and cumulative sun exposure. *   More common in individuals living closer to the equator. *   **Gender**: More prevalent in males, likely due to higher rates of cumulative occupational and recreational sun exposure. *   **Race**: Significantly more common in fair-skinned individuals (Fitzpatrick skin types I and II).  ---
riskFactors: **Primary Risk Factor**: Chronic, cumulative sun exposure.
**Host Factors**:
*   Fitzpatrick skin types I and II (fair skin, light hair/eyes, easily burns).
*   Increasing age.
*   Male gender.
*   Personal history of AK or other skin cancers (BCC, SCC, melanoma).
**Medical Factors**:

*   **Immunosuppression**: Organ transplant recipients, patients on chronic immunosuppressive therapy, and those with hematologic malignancies (e.g., CLL) have a drastically increased risk of AK and progression to SCC.
*   Genetic syndromes predisposing to UV damage (e.g., xeroderma pigmentosum, albinism).
**Other Exposures**:
*   Ionizing radiation.
*   Arsenic exposure.
*   Phototherapy (e.g., PUVA).
DERM__malignancy__actinic_keratosis.clinicalPresentation: *   Patients typically present with one or more small, rough spots on chronically sun-exposed areas. *   Common locations: **face, scalp (especially in bald men), ears (helices), neck, dorsal forearms, and hands**. *   Lesions are often discovered incidentally during an exam or because the patient notes a persistent rough or scaly area. *   Multiple lesions are common.  ---
symptoms: Often **asymptomatic**.
May be pruritic, tender, or have a stinging sensation.
Patients often describe the lesion as a "rough patch" or "sandpaper spot" that may intermittently flake off and recur.
examFindings: **Palpation**: Often **"better felt than seen."** The key finding is a **rough, sandpaper-like texture** on palpation.
**Inspection**:
*   **Morphology**: Solitary or multiple, ill-defined erythematous macules, papules, or plaques.
*   **Scale**: Adherent, hyperkeratotic scale that can be yellow, white, or dirty brown.
*   **Size**: Typically ranges from 3 to 10 mm.
*   **Base**: The base of the lesion is typically erythematous (pink or red).
**Special Variants**:
*   **Cutaneous Horn**: A conical, dense, hyperkeratotic projection. The base of a cutaneous horn can harbor an AK or an underlying SCC, warranting biopsy.

*   **Actinic Cheilitis**: AK occurring on the vermilion border of the lip, most commonly the **lower lip**. Presents as persistent dryness, scaling, and blurring of the lip margin. Has a higher rate of progression to SCC than cutaneous AK.
*   **Pigmented AK**: Contains melanin, appearing as a brownish papule. Must be differentiated from lentigo maligna.
treatment: **Lesion-Directed Therapies**:
*   **Cryotherapy (Liquid Nitrogen)**: Most common treatment for isolated lesions. Causes localized blistering and crusting, with resolution in 1-2 weeks.
*   **Curettage +/- Electrodessication**: Scraping the lesion off with a curette.
**Field-Directed Therapies**:

*   **Topical Fluorouracil (5-FU)**: A pyrimidine analog that inhibits DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells. Applied for several weeks, causes marked inflammation, erythema, and erosions before healing. High efficacy.
*   **Topical Imiquimod**: An immune response modifier that stimulates a local immune reaction against the atypical cells. Also causes a significant inflammatory response.

*   **Photodynamic Therapy (PDT)**: Application of a topical photosensitizer (e.g., aminolevulinic acid) followed by exposure to a specific wavelength of light (blue or red light), which selectively destroys the atypical cells.
*   **Topical Diclofenac**: A topical NSAID, less irritating than 5-FU or imiquimod but may be less effective.
*   **Chemical Peels / Laser Resurfacing**: Can be effective for widespread facial AKs.
management: **Patient Education is CRITICAL**:
*   **Sun Protection**: Emphasize daily use of broad-spectrum sunscreen (SPF 30+), wearing sun-protective clothing (hats, long sleeves), and avoiding peak sun hours (10 am - 4 pm).
*   **Skin Self-Exams**: Teach patients to monitor their skin for new or changing lesions, focusing on the "red flags" for SCC.
**Follow-up**: Regular full-body skin examinations are crucial.
*   Frequency: Every 6-12 months, or more frequently for high-risk patients (immunosuppressed, history of multiple skin cancers).
complications: The most significant complication is **progression to Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)**.
*   The risk per lesion per year is low (~0.1-1%), but the cumulative lifetime risk for a patient with multiple AKs is significant (up to 10%).
*   SCC arising from AK is typically low-grade, but has the potential for metastasis.
Other complications include pain, bleeding, secondary infection, and cosmetic disfigurement from the lesions or their treatment.
DERM__malignancy__actinic_keratosis.prognosis: *   The prognosis for individual AKs treated appropriately is excellent. *   However, the presence of AKs serves as a powerful marker for significant cumulative sun damage, placing the patient at a **lifelong increased risk for developing SCC, BCC, and melanoma**. *   Prognosis is worse in immunosuppressed patients, who have a much higher rate of progression to aggressive SCC.  ---

diagnostics.notes: *   **Definitive Diagnosis:** **Biopsy with histopathology**. *   **Biopsy Technique:** *   **Shave biopsy** is the most common and preferred method for most suspected BCCs. *   **Punch biopsy** can be used for flat or pigmented lesions. *   **Dermoscopy:** A handheld tool used to magnify and illuminate the skin, revealing specific features not visible to the naked eye (e.g., arborizing vessels, blue-gray ovoid nests, spoke wheel areas). *   **Histopathology Findings:** Nests of **basaloid cells** with scant cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nuclei, showing **peripheral palisading** (nuclei at the edge of nests align in a row) and **stromal retraction** (clefts/spaces between the tumor and surrounding stroma).

DERM__malignancy__basal_cell_carcinoma.overview: Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC) is the **most common human malignancy**. It is a non-melanoma skin cancer arising from the basal cells of the epidermis and its adnexal structures (hair follicles). BCC is characterized by slow growth, local invasion, and a very low rate of metastasis. It typically appears on sun-exposed skin.
DERM__malignancy__basal_cell_carcinoma.etiologyPathophysiology: *   **Etiology:** The primary cause is DNA damage from **ultraviolet (UV) radiation**, particularly UVB. Other causes include ionizing radiation, arsenic exposure, and genetic predisposition. *   **Pathophysiology:** *   UV radiation induces the formation of pyrimidine dimers in DNA, leading to mutations. *   The key pathway involved is the **Hedgehog (Hh) signaling pathway**. *   Mutations, most commonly in the **PTCH1 (Patched-1) tumor suppressor gene**, lead to uncontrolled activation of this pathway. *   This dysregulation results in the uncontrolled proliferation of basaloid cells, forming the tumor.
DERM__malignancy__basal_cell_carcinoma.epidemiology: *   **Most common cancer worldwide.** *   Incidence: >4 million cases diagnosed annually in the U.S. *   More common in **males** than females. *   Incidence increases sharply with age, typically affecting individuals **> 50 years old**. *   Higher prevalence in fair-skinned individuals (Fitzpatrick skin types I and II) and in geographic locations with high sun exposure (closer to the equator, higher altitudes).
DERM__malignancy__basal_cell_carcinoma.clinicalPresentation: BCC has several clinical subtypes, each with a distinct appearance:  1.  **Nodular BCC (Most Common: ~60%)** *   Classically a **pink or flesh-colored papule** with a **pearly or translucent** quality. *   Often has overlying **telangiectasias** (small, dilated blood vessels). *   May have a **rolled border** and central ulceration (often called a **"rodent ulcer"**). *   Most common on the head and neck, especially the nose.  2.  **Superficial BCC (~30%)** *   Appears as a pink or red, slightly scaly patch or plaque. *   May have a fine, thread-like, slightly raised border. *   Often mistaken for eczema, psoriasis, or actinic keratosis. *   Most common on the trunk and extremities.  3.  **Morpheaform / Sclerosing / Infiltrative BCC (~5-10%)** *   The most aggressive subtype. *   Appears as a white, yellow, or flesh-colored, scar-like plaque. *   Borders are often ill-defined and indistinct. *   Firm, indurated, and may be depressed below the skin surface. *   High risk for recurrence due to subclinical extension.  4.  **Pigmented BCC** *   Similar to nodular BCC but contains melanin (brown, blue, or black pigment). *   Can be mistaken for malignant melanoma. Key differentiating features are the presence of a pearly sheen, rolled border, and telangiectasias.
DERM__malignancy__basal_cell_carcinoma.prognosis: *   **Excellent** for the vast majority of cases. *   The 5-year cure rate with appropriate treatment is **>95%**. *   Mortality is extremely low and is almost always due to uncontrolled local invasion or rare metastasis from a neglected, aggressive tumor.
riskFactors: Chronic and intermittent intense ultraviolet (UV) light exposure (most significant factor)
Fair skin phototypes (Fitzpatrick I/II), light-colored eyes, and red/blond hair
History of frequent or severe sunburns, particularly in childhood
Increasing age and male gender
Personal history of any skin cancer (BCC, SCC, or melanoma)
Immunosuppression (e.g., solid organ transplant recipients, chronic lymphocytic leukemia)
Genetic syndromes (e.g., Gorlin syndrome/Nevoid BCC Syndrome, Xeroderma Pigmentosum)
Previous exposure to ionizing radiation (e.g., radiation therapy for acne or cancer)
Chronic arsenic exposure
Chronic scarring or inflammation (e.g., Marjolin's ulcer in a burn scar)
symptoms: Often asymptomatic
A persistent, non-healing sore that may bleed, ooze, or crust
A lesion that bleeds easily with minor trauma (e.g., shaving or toweling)
A new skin growth that appears pearly, waxy, translucent, or scar-like
Slow but relentless growth of a lesion over months to years
Less commonly, pruritus or localized tenderness
examFindings: Nodular BCC (most common): Pearly or translucent papule or nodule with a rolled border and overlying fine telangiectasias. May have central ulceration ('rodent ulcer').
Superficial BCC: Erythematous, well-demarcated, scaly patch or thin plaque, often with a thread-like, pearly border. Commonly found on the trunk and extremities.

Morpheaform/Sclerotic BCC: An ill-defined, indurated, firm, scar-like plaque that is flesh-colored or yellowish. Borders are difficult to discern clinically, indicating aggressive, subclinical extension.
Pigmented BCC: Contains melanin, appearing as a brown, blue, or black lesion. May mimic nodular melanoma but often retains some classic features like a pearly border or telangiectasias.
Fibroepithelioma of Pinkus: Rare variant, presenting as a firm, flesh-colored or pink papule, typically on the lumbosacral area.
treatment: Treatment choice is guided by tumor subtype, size, location (high vs. low-risk areas), and patient factors.
Surgical (Highest Cure Rates):

- Mohs Micrographic Surgery: Gold standard for high-risk tumors (face, ears, hands, feet), recurrent tumors, aggressive histologic subtypes (morpheaform, infiltrative), or for maximal tissue conservation. Offers ~99% cure rate.
- Standard Surgical Excision: Treatment of choice for low-risk BCCs, involving excision with 4-5 mm clinical margins.
- Curettage and Electrodesiccation (C&D): For small, low-risk, well-defined tumors on the trunk and extremities in non-hair-bearing areas.
Non-Surgical:
- Radiation Therapy: Primary option for poor surgical candidates or as adjuvant therapy for tumors with perineural invasion.
- Topical Therapies (for superficial BCC): Imiquimod cream, 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) cream.
- Cryosurgery: For small, low-risk primary BCCs.
- Photodynamic Therapy (PDT): For superficial BCCs.
Systemic Therapy (for locally advanced or metastatic BCC):
- Hedgehog Pathway Inhibitors (e.g., Vismodegib, Sonidegib).
management: Patient Education: Counsel on rigorous sun protection, including use of broad-spectrum sunscreen (SPF 30+), sun-protective clothing, and avoidance of peak sun hours (10 a.m. to 4 p.m.).
Skin Self-Examination: Educate patients to perform monthly full-body self-examinations to detect new or changing lesions early.

Clinical Surveillance: Regular full-body skin examinations by a clinician. Recommended frequency is every 6-12 months for the first 5 years, then annually, as patients have a >40% risk of developing a new non-melanoma skin cancer within 5 years.
complications: Local Tissue Destruction: If left untreated, BCC can invade and destroy adjacent skin, cartilage, muscle, and bone, causing significant functional impairment and cosmetic disfigurement, especially on the face.
Recurrence: Risk is higher for tumors with aggressive histologic subtypes, perineural invasion, large size, or those in high-risk locations.
Perineural Invasion (PNI): Spread of tumor along nerves, associated with higher recurrence rates and potential for pain, numbness, or muscle weakness.
Metastasis: Extremely rare (<0.1%) but possible, typically in very large, neglected, or recurrent tumors. Common sites are regional lymph nodes, lungs, and bones.
Treatment-Related Morbidity: Scarring, pigmentary alteration, infection, bleeding, and nerve damage from surgical or destructive procedures.

diagnostics.notes: *   **Gold Standard**: **Biopsy with histopathology**. *   **Biopsy Technique**: *   **Shave Biopsy**: Suitable for superficial, papular lesions. *   **Punch Biopsy**: Preferred for plaques or nodules to assess depth of invasion. *   **Excisional Biopsy**: Can be diagnostic and therapeutic for smaller, well-defined lesions. *   **Histopathology Findings**: *   Invasion of atypical, pleomorphic keratinocytes into the dermis or beyond. *   Cells feature large, hyperchromatic nuclei and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. *   **Keratin pearls**: Pathognomonic finding of well-differentiated SCC, appearing as eosinophilic, concentric layers of squamous cells with central keratinization.

DERM__malignancy__squamous_cell_carcinom.overview: Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC) is the **second most common type of skin cancer** after Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC). It is a malignant proliferation of suprabasal epidermal keratinocytes. While most cases of cutaneous SCC (cSCC) are localized and have a high cure rate, a subset can be aggressive, with potential for local recurrence, perineural invasion, and distant metastasis. The most common precursor lesion is **Actinic Keratosis (AK)**.
DERM__malignancy__squamous_cell_carcinom.etiologyPathophysiology: *   **Etiology**: The primary cause is cumulative exposure to **ultraviolet (UV) radiation**, particularly UVB. UV light induces DNA damage, primarily causing pyrimidine dimers, which leads to mutations in key regulatory genes. *   **Pathophysiology**: The most commonly mutated gene in SCC is the **TP53 tumor suppressor gene**. This mutation disrupts normal cell cycle control and apoptosis (programmed cell death), allowing for the uncontrolled proliferation of atypical keratinocytes. *   **Other Causes**: *   **Human Papillomavirus (HPV)**: Especially in anogenital and periungual SCC. *   **Chronic Inflammation/Scarring**: SCC can arise in chronic wounds, burns, or scars (**Marjolin's Ulcer**). *   **Immunosuppression**: Impaired immune surveillance significantly increases risk. *   **Carcinogen Exposure**: Arsenic, industrial tars, radiation.
DERM__malignancy__squamous_cell_carcinom.epidemiology: *   **Incidence**: Second most common skin cancer, with over 1 million cases diagnosed annually in the U.S. *   **Affected Population**: Primarily affects older individuals (>50 years). *   **Sex**: More common in males than females (approx. 2:1 ratio), likely due to higher cumulative sun exposure. *   **Risk Groups**: Highest incidence in fair-skinned individuals (Fitzpatrick types I and II) living in areas with high sun exposure.
riskFactors: **UV Exposure**: History of extensive sun exposure, sunburns, or tanning bed use.
**Phenotype**: Fair skin, light hair, blue/green eyes (Fitzpatrick I-II).
**Immunosuppression**: **Organ transplant recipients** are at a ~65-250 fold increased risk. Patients with HIV or chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) are also at high risk.
**Precursor Lesions**: **Actinic Keratosis (AK)**, Bowen's disease (SCC in situ).
**Chronic Wounds**: Non-healing ulcers, burn scars, osteomyelitis sinus tracts.
**Genetic Syndromes**: Xeroderma pigmentosum, Oculocutaneous Albinism.
**History**: Personal or family history of skin cancer.
**Ionizing Radiation**: Prior radiation therapy.
DERM__malignancy__squamous_cell_carcinom.clinicalPresentation: *   The classic presentation is a **non-healing, growing lesion** in a sun-exposed area that may bleed with minimal trauma. *   Lesions are typically found on the head, neck, forearms, and dorsal hands. *   SCC can present in several forms: *   **Papule or Plaque**: Erythematous, indurated (firm), and scaly. *   **Nodule**: Firm, hyperkeratotic, may have a central ulceration. *   **Ulcer**: A persistent, shallow or excavated sore with a red base and firm, raised borders. *   **Cutaneous Horn**: A conical, dense, hyperkeratotic projection.
symptoms: Often asymptomatic.
**Pruritus** (itching)
**Tenderness or pain**, especially with perineural invasion.
**Bleeding** that is spontaneous or follows minor trauma (friable).
A sensation of a "sore that doesn't heal."
examFindings: **Inspection**:
*   **Morphology**: Erythematous, indurated papule, plaque, or nodule.
*   **Surface**: Typically has overlying scale, crust, hyperkeratosis, or ulceration.
*   **Borders**: Often ill-defined.
**Palpation**:
*   **Induration**: The lesion feels firm, thickened, and deep upon palpation.
*   **Fixation**: Check if the lesion is mobile or fixed to underlying structures.
*   **Regional Lymphadenopathy**: Palpate regional lymph nodes (e.g., cervical, preauricular, axillary, inguinal) to assess for potential metastasis.
treatment: **Surgical (First-Line)**

*   **Mohs Micrographic Surgery**: Highest cure rate (~99%) and maximal tissue preservation. **Treatment of choice** for high-risk SCCs (face, ears, hands, feet), large or recurrent tumors, or in immunosuppressed patients.
*   **Standard Surgical Excision**: Used for lower-risk tumors in non-critical areas. Requires 4-6 mm clinical margins.
**Destructive Methods**
*   **Curettage & Electrodesiccation (C&E)**: For small, low-risk, primary tumors in non-critical sites.
*   **Cryotherapy**: Primarily for precursor lesions (AK) or SCC in situ (Bowen's disease).
**Non-Surgical**
*   **Radiation Therapy**: For non-surgical candidates or as adjuvant therapy for high-risk tumors (e.g., with perineural invasion).
*   **Topical Therapy (for SCC in situ)**: Topical 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU), Imiquimod.
**Systemic Therapy (for metastatic disease)**: Immunotherapy (e.g., PD-1 inhibitors like Cemiplimab, Pembrolizumab) or chemotherapy.
management: **Follow-up**: Essential for early detection of recurrence or new primary skin cancers.
*   **High-Risk SCC**: Full body skin exams every 3-6 months for 2 years, then annually.
*   **Low-Risk SCC**: Full body skin exams every 6-12 months for 2 years, then annually.
**Patient Education**:
*   **Sun Protection**: Emphasize broad-spectrum sunscreen (SPF 30+), sun-protective clothing, hats, and avoidance of peak sun hours (10 am - 4 pm).
*   **Self-Skin Exams**: Teach patients to perform monthly self-exams to identify new or changing lesions.
complications: **Local Recurrence**: Higher risk with inadequate excision or high-risk features.
**Metastasis**: Risk is ~3-5%. Most common site is regional lymph nodes. Distant metastases (lung, liver, brain) are rare but carry a poor prognosis.
**Perineural Invasion (PNI)**: Tumor cells track along nerves. Associated with pain, numbness, and higher recurrence rates.
**Cosmetic/Functional Deficit**: Resulting from large tumors or extensive surgical excision, especially on the face or hands.
DERM__malignancy__squamous_cell_carcinom.prognosis: *   **Excellent** for most localized cutaneous SCC, with a 5-year cure rate >95% with appropriate treatment. *   **Prognosis worsens** with high-risk features: *   **Size**: >2 cm in diameter. *   **Depth**: Invasion beyond the subcutaneous fat. *   **Location**: Ear, lip, central face. *   **Histology**: Poorly differentiated. *   **Etiology**: Arising in a scar or chronic wound (Marjolin's ulcer). *   **Host**: Immunosuppression. *   **Metastatic SCC**: 5-year survival rate drops significantly to <50%.

diagnostics.notes: *   **Biopsy is mandatory for any suspicious lesion.** *   **Gold Standard:** **Full-thickness excisional biopsy** with 1-3 mm clinical margins. This technique allows the pathologist to measure the full tumor depth (Breslow thickness) without transecting the base. *   **Alternatives:** A deep shave (saucerization) or a punch biopsy may be used for large lesions or cosmetically sensitive areas, but it must be deep enough to include the reticular dermis. A superficial shave biopsy is inadequate and should be avoided. *   **Histopathology Report:** Key prognostic information includes: *   **Breslow Thickness (in mm):** The single most important prognostic factor. Measured from the granular layer of the epidermis to the deepest point of tumor invasion. *   **Ulceration:** Presence or absence is a powerful, independent prognostic factor. *   **Mitotic Rate:** Number of mitoses per square millimeter (mitoses/mm2). *   **Clark Level:** Anatomic level of invasion (less commonly used for staging now but may be reported). *   Presence of lymphovascular invasion, microsatellites, and regression. *   **Staging Workup (for invasive melanoma):** *   **Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy (SLNB):** Recommended for melanomas with Breslow depth >0.8 mm or those <0.8 mm with adverse features (e.g., ulceration, high mitotic rate). The status of the sentinel node is the most important prognostic factor for patients without clinical metastasis. *   **Imaging:** For patients with positive nodes or signs of distant disease (Stage III/IV), imaging such as PET/CT, CT of chest/abdomen/pelvis, and/or brain MRI is used. *   **Labs:** Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is a prognostic marker in metastatic disease. *   **Molecular Testing:** Tumor tissue is tested for **BRAF V600E** and other mutations (NRAS, c-KIT) to guide systemic therapy in advanced disease.

DERM__malignancy__melanoma.overview: Melanoma is a malignant neoplasm of melanocytes, the pigment-producing cells derived from the neural crest. While it accounts for less than 5% of all skin cancers, it is responsible for the vast majority of skin cancer-related deaths due to its high potential for early metastasis. It can arise from a pre-existing nevus or de novo. The most common locations are sun-exposed skin, but it can also occur in non-sun-exposed areas, mucous membranes, the uveal tract of the eye, and the leptomeninges.
DERM__malignancy__melanoma.etiologyPathophysiology: Melanoma develops from the malignant transformation of melanocytes. The primary etiologic agent is ultraviolet (UV) radiation exposure, particularly UVA and UVB.  *   **UVB (290-320 nm):** Directly damages melanocyte DNA, causing the formation of cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers (CPDs), leading to signature C>T or CC>TT mutations. *   **UVA (320-400 nm):** Generates reactive oxygen species, causing oxidative DNA damage. *   **Genetic Mutations:** A stepwise accumulation of genetic mutations leads to malignant transformation and progression. Key pathways involved: *   **MAP Kinase Pathway:** Activating mutations are common. *   **BRAF (V600E):** Most common mutation (~50% of cutaneous melanomas). Leads to constitutive activation of the signaling pathway, promoting cell proliferation. *   **NRAS:** Second most common (~20%). *   **Tumor Suppressor Genes:** Inactivating mutations. *   **CDKN2A:** Encodes p16 (cell cycle inhibitor); germline mutations are associated with familial melanoma (Familial Atypical Multiple Mole Melanoma *   FAMMM syndrome). *   **PTEN:** Inactivation is also common. *   **Growth Phases:** *   **Radial (Horizontal) Growth Phase:** Malignant cells proliferate laterally within the epidermis and superficial dermis. Little to no metastatic potential. *   **Vertical Growth Phase:** Cells invade downwards into the deeper dermis and gain access to blood vessels and lymphatics, conferring metastatic potential. This is the critical step for disease progression.
DERM__malignancy__melanoma.epidemiology: *   Incidence is rising faster than any other preventable cancer in the United States. *   It is one of the most common cancers in young adults (especially women aged 25-29). *   Overall incidence is higher in men than in women. *   Significantly more common in fair-skinned individuals (Fitzpatrick skin types I and II) and those living closer to the equator. *   Less common in individuals with darker skin (Fitzpatrick V and VI), but when it occurs, it is often in non-sun-exposed areas (e.g., acral or mucosal) and is frequently diagnosed at a later, more advanced stage.
DERM__malignancy__melanoma.clinicalPresentation: The presentation varies based on the melanoma subtype. The most common sign is a new or changing skin lesion.  *   **Superficial Spreading Melanoma (SSM):** *   **Most common type (~70%).** *   Often arises in a pre-existing nevus. *   Long radial growth phase before vertical invasion. *   Typically presents as a flat or slightly elevated macule or plaque with irregular borders and color variegation. *   **Nodular Melanoma:** *   **Second most common type (~15-20%).** *   Aggressive, with early vertical growth and poor prognosis. *   Presents as a rapidly growing, darkly pigmented (blue-black), dome-shaped or pedunculated papule or nodule. Often uniform in color. May ulcerate and bleed easily. *   **Lentigo Maligna Melanoma:** *   ~5-10% of cases. *   Occurs in older individuals on chronically sun-damaged skin (face, neck, forearms). *   Begins as a tan or brown macule (lentigo maligna or "Hutchinson's freckle") that slowly enlarges over years (long radial growth phase) before developing a nodular component (invasion). *   **Acral Lentiginous Melanoma:** *   <5% of cases, but the **most common type in darker-skinned individuals** (African Americans, Asians, Hispanics). *   Arises on palms, soles, and beneath the nail plate (subungual). *   Often presents as a dark brown/black, irregularly shaped macule or patch. *   Subungual melanoma may present as a longitudinal melanonychia (dark streak in the nail) that widens or involves the nail fold (**Hutchinson's sign**). *   **Amelanotic Melanoma:** *   ~5% of cases; lacks pigment. *   Presents as a pink, red, or flesh-colored papule or nodule. *   Often misdiagnosed as basal cell carcinoma, pyogenic granuloma, or a benign inflammatory lesion, leading to delayed diagnosis and a worse prognosis.
DERM__malignancy__melanoma.prognosis: *   Prognosis is excellent for thin, localized melanomas and poor for advanced, metastatic disease. *   **Key Prognostic Factors (in order of importance for localized disease):** 1.  **Breslow Thickness:** The single most important factor. Thicker tumors have a worse prognosis. 2.  **Tumor Ulceration:** Presence is a poor prognostic sign. 3.  **Sentinel Lymph Node Status:** Positive SLN significantly worsens prognosis. 4.  **Mitotic Rate:** Higher rate indicates more rapid proliferation and worse prognosis. *   **5-Year Survival Rates (Approximate):** *   Localized (Stage I/II): >95% *   Regional (Stage III): ~60-70% *   Distant (Stage IV): ~25-30%
riskFactors: Personal history of melanoma (strongest risk factor for a second primary).
Family history of melanoma in a first-degree relative.
Presence of multiple atypical (dysplastic) nevi.
High total body nevus count (>50-100).
Presence of a large congenital melanocytic nevus.
Phenotypic traits: Fair skin (Fitzpatrick type I/II), light-colored eyes, red/blond hair, freckling.
History of intense, intermittent UV exposure and blistering sunburns, particularly in childhood.
Use of indoor tanning devices.
Genetic predisposition (e.g., germline mutations in CDKN2A associated with FAMMM syndrome).
Immunosuppression (e.g., solid organ transplant recipients, chronic lymphocytic leukemia).
symptoms: Most commonly, a new or changing pigmented lesion on the skin.
The lesion may be asymptomatic or associated with pruritus (itching), which is a common early symptom.
Bleeding, ulceration, or crusting of a pre-existing or new mole.
Tenderness or pain in a lesion (less common, often a later sign).
A sore that fails to heal.

Symptoms of metastatic disease may include: new palpable lymphadenopathy, unexplained weight loss, fatigue, headaches/seizures (brain metastasis), shortness of breath/cough (lung metastasis), or abdominal pain/jaundice (liver metastasis).
examFindings: **ABCDE criteria** for suspicious pigmented lesions:
- **A**symmetry: One half of the lesion is unlike the other.
- **B**order: Irregular, scalloped, or poorly defined.
- **C**olor: Variegation; multiple shades of brown, black, tan, or presence of blue, red, or white.
- **D**iameter: Typically >6 mm, though smaller melanomas can occur.
- **E**volving: A lesion that is changing in size, shape, color, or elevation.
The **'Ugly Duckling' sign**: A mole that looks distinctly different from the patient's other moles.
**Clinical Subtypes:**
- **Superficial Spreading:** Most common; presents as a flat macule or patch that develops into a plaque with irregular borders and color variegation.
- **Nodular:** Rapidly growing papule or nodule, often symmetric, and may be blue-black, pink, or red (amelanotic). Prone to early ulceration and vertical growth.
- **Lentigo Maligna:** Occurs on chronically sun-damaged skin (e.g., face, neck) as a large, slowly enlarging, flat, tan-brown macule with irregular borders.

- **Acral Lentiginous:** Arises on palms, soles, or under the nails (subungual). Subungual melanoma may present as a new longitudinal melanonychia (dark band) with pigment extending to the nail fold (**Hutchinson's sign**).
Examination should include a full-body skin check and palpation of regional lymph node basins (cervical, axillary, inguinal) for lymphadenopathy.
treatment: **Localized Disease (Stage 0-II):**

- **Wide Local Excision (WLE):** The standard of care. Surgical margins are determined by Breslow thickness: 0.5-1 cm for in situ, 1 cm for tumors <1 mm, 1-2 cm for tumors 1-2 mm, and 2 cm for tumors >2 mm.
- **Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy (SLNB):** A staging procedure performed with WLE for tumors >0.8 mm thick or those with other high-risk features (e.g., ulceration).
**Regional Disease (Stage III):**
- **Surgical Management:** May include completion lymph node dissection for clinically positive nodes.
- **Adjuvant Systemic Therapy:** Post-surgical treatment to reduce recurrence risk in high-risk Stage IIB/C and Stage III patients.
- **Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors:** Anti-PD-1 agents (Nivolumab, Pembrolizumab).
- **Targeted Therapy (for BRAF-mutated tumors):** Combination BRAF/MEK inhibitors (e.g., Dabrafenib/Trametinib).
**Metastatic Disease (Stage IV):**
- **Systemic Therapy is the mainstay:**
- **First-line Immunotherapy:** Combination anti-PD-1 (Nivolumab) + anti-CTLA-4 (Ipilimumab) or anti-PD-1 monotherapy.
- **Targeted Therapy:** For BRAF V600-mutated melanoma, combination BRAF/MEK inhibitors provide rapid responses.
- **Palliative Care:** Radiation therapy for symptomatic bone or brain metastases; surgical resection for isolated metastases.
management: **Long-term Surveillance:** Lifelong follow-up is essential and is risk-stratified by stage.
- **Patient Education:** Counsel on strict sun protection (sunscreen, protective clothing, avoidance of peak sun hours) and performing monthly self-skin exams.
- **Clinical Follow-up:** Regular full-body skin examinations and lymph node palpation by a dermatologist. Frequency ranges from every 3-6 months to annually, depending on the stage at diagnosis.
- **Imaging Surveillance:** For patients with high-risk disease (Stage IIB and higher), periodic imaging (e.g., CT or PET/CT scans) may be used to monitor for recurrence or metastasis.
**Genetic Counseling:** Consider for patients with a strong family history, multiple primary melanomas, or early-onset disease to assess for germline mutations like CDKN2A.
**Psychosocial Support:** Address the psychological impact of a cancer diagnosis, including anxiety about recurrence.
complications: **Disease-Related:**
- **Local or In-transit Recurrence:** Reappearance of melanoma at or near the primary site.
- **Metastasis:** Spread to regional lymph nodes, lung, liver, brain, bone, and skin, which is the primary cause of mortality.
- **Second Primary Melanoma:** Patients have an approximately 5-10% lifetime risk of developing a new primary melanoma.
**Treatment-Related:**
- **Surgical Complications:** Scarring, infection, nerve damage, and lymphedema (especially after axillary or inguinal lymph node dissection).

- **Immunotherapy Side Effects (irAEs):** Immune-related adverse events can cause inflammation in any organ, including colitis, hepatitis, pneumonitis, dermatitis, and endocrinopathies (e.g., thyroiditis, hypophysitis).
- **Targeted Therapy Side Effects:** Fevers (pyrexia), rash, photosensitivity, arthralgias, and rarely, cardiomyopathy or secondary skin cancers (e.g., squamous cell carcinoma).

diagnostics.notes: 1.  **Biopsy (Definitive Diagnosis):** *   A **full-thickness biopsy** (deep punch, incisional, or excisional) is required. *   **Shave biopsies are inadequate** as they do not allow for assessment of tumor depth or lymphovascular invasion. *   **Histology:** Shows sheets of small, round, blue cells with scant cytoplasm, granular chromatin ("salt and pepper"), a high mitotic rate, and frequent necrosis. 2.  **Immunohistochemistry (IHC):** *   Essential to differentiate MCC from other small round blue cell tumors. *   **Positive (+): Cytokeratin 20 (CK-20)** in a characteristic **perinuclear dot-like pattern**. This is highly specific. *   **Positive (+):** Neuroendocrine markers such as **Synaptophysin**, **Chromogranin A**, and Neuron-Specific Enolase (NSE). *   **Negative (-):** Thyroid Transcription Factor-1 (TTF-1) - helps rule out small cell lung cancer metastasis. *   **Negative (-):** S-100 - helps rule out melanoma. *   **Negative (-):** Leukocyte Common Antigen (LCA) - helps rule out lymphoma. 3.  **Staging Workup (Essential):** *   **Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy (SLNB):** Recommended for ALL patients with clinically negative nodes. There is a high rate (~30%) of occult (microscopic) nodal metastasis. *   **Imaging:** Cross-sectional imaging is mandatory to assess for distant disease. *   **PET/CT scan** is the preferred modality. *   CT of the chest/abdomen/pelvis with contrast is an alternative. *   Brain MRI if neurologic symptoms are present.

DERM__malignancy__merkel_cell_carcinoma.overview: Merkel Cell Carcinoma (MCC) is a rare but highly aggressive primary neuroendocrine carcinoma of the skin. It has a high propensity for local recurrence, regional lymph node metastasis, and distant spread. It typically presents as a rapidly growing, painless, reddish-purple nodule on sun-exposed skin in elderly, fair-skinned, or immunosuppressed individuals. Diagnosis is confirmed by biopsy with specific immunohistochemical staining. Management is multidisciplinary and requires aggressive staging and treatment.
DERM__malignancy__merkel_cell_carcinoma.etiologyPathophysiology: There are two primary, distinct etiologic pathways for MCC development:  1.  **Viral Pathogenesis (~80% of cases):** *   Caused by the integration of the **Merkel Cell Polyomavirus (MCPyV)** into the host cell's DNA. *   MCPyV is a common, usually asymptomatic virus in the general population. *   In MCC, a clonal integration of the viral genome occurs, leading to the expression of viral oncoproteins (Large T and Small T antigens). *   These oncoproteins inactivate host tumor suppressor proteins, primarily the **Retinoblastoma protein (pRb)**, driving uncontrolled cell proliferation. *   Virus-positive tumors typically have a low tumor mutational burden.  2.  **UV-Induced Pathogenesis (~20% of cases):** *   Caused by extensive DNA damage from chronic ultraviolet (UV) radiation exposure. *   These tumors are MCPyV-negative. *   They are characterized by a very **high tumor mutational burden** with a classic "UV signature" (C>T transitions). *   Mutations in key tumor suppressor genes like **TP53** and **RB1** are common.  The cell of origin is debated but is thought to be a dermal fibroblast or an early B-cell progenitor, not the Merkel cell itself.
DERM__malignancy__merkel_cell_carcinoma.epidemiology: *   **Incidence:** Rare, approximately 0.7 cases per 100,000 person-years in the U.S., but the incidence is rapidly increasing. *   **Age:** Primarily a disease of the elderly; median age at diagnosis is **~75 years**. *   **Sex:** Slight male predominance (approx. 1.5:1). *   **Race:** Overwhelmingly affects **Caucasians** and fair-skinned individuals (Fitzpatrick types I-II).
DERM__malignancy__merkel_cell_carcinoma.clinicalPresentation: The classic presentation is a solitary, rapidly growing nodule on sun-exposed skin, most commonly the **head and neck (~50%)**, followed by the extremities and trunk. The lesion often goes unnoticed or is misdiagnosed initially due to its non-specific appearance.
DERM__malignancy__merkel_cell_carcinoma.prognosis: Prognosis is heavily dependent on the stage at diagnosis. MCC is more lethal than melanoma at comparable stages. *   **Overall 5-Year Survival:** ~60% *   **Stage I:** ~80% *   **Stage II:** ~60% *   **Stage III (Nodal Disease):** ~40-50% *   **Stage IV (Distant Metastasis):** <20%  Negative prognostic factors include male sex, immunosuppression, large tumor size, and truncal location.
riskFactors: Advanced age (>65 years)
Chronic ultraviolet (UV) radiation exposure (e.g., history of sunbathing, tanning beds, PUVA therapy)
Fair skin phototype (Fitzpatrick I-II)
Chronic immunosuppression (e.g., solid organ transplant recipients, chronic lymphocytic leukemia [CLL], HIV/AIDS)
History of other skin cancers (e.g., basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma)
Merkel Cell Polyomavirus (MCPyV) infection (a necessary but not sufficient factor for viral-pathway MCC)
symptoms: A rapidly growing, firm, painless skin nodule or plaque.
The clinical features are often summarized by the 'AEIOU' mnemonic: Asymptomatic, Expanding rapidly, Immunosuppression, Older than 50, and UV-exposed site.
The lesion is typically red, violaceous, or flesh-colored.
The overlying skin is often shiny and may have telangiectasias; ulceration is a late finding.
Symptoms of nodal or distant metastasis may be present, such as a new palpable lump in a nodal basin, fatigue, or unexplained weight loss.
examFindings: A solitary, firm, non-tender, dome-shaped nodule or indurated plaque.
Color ranges from flesh-toned to pink, red, or purple/violaceous.
Located most commonly on sun-exposed skin, with the head and neck being the most frequent site, followed by the extremities and trunk.
Thorough examination of regional lymph node basins (e.g., cervical, axillary, inguinal) is critical, as palpable lymphadenopathy may be present in up to 30% of patients at presentation.
treatment: Treatment is multidisciplinary, involving surgical oncology, radiation oncology, and medical oncology.
**Localized/Regional Disease (Stage I-III):**
1. **Wide Local Excision (WLE):** Surgical removal of the primary tumor with 1-2 cm clinical margins.
2. **Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy (SLNB):** Standard of care for all clinically node-negative patients to stage the regional basin.
3. **Adjuvant Radiation Therapy (RT):** Commonly recommended to the primary tumor bed and/or the nodal basin (if SLNB is positive or in high-risk cases) to decrease locoregional recurrence.
4. **Complete Lymph Node Dissection (CLND):** Performed for a positive SLNB or clinically palpable nodes.
**Metastatic/Unresectable Disease (Stage IV):**
1. **Immunotherapy (First-Line):** Immune checkpoint inhibitors targeting the PD-1/PD-L1 axis (e.g., Avelumab, Pembrolizumab) are the standard of care, showing durable responses.

2. **Chemotherapy (Second-Line):** Traditional cytotoxic agents (e.g., carboplatin/etoposide) are reserved for patients who progress on or are ineligible for immunotherapy; responses are typically short-lived.
3. **Palliative Radiation:** Can be used for symptomatic control of metastatic lesions.
management: Due to the high risk of recurrence, aggressive post-treatment surveillance is mandatory.
**Follow-up Schedule:** Lifelong follow-up with frequent physical examinations (full skin and nodal exam) every 3-6 months for the first 2-3 years, then every 6-12 months thereafter.

**Surveillance Imaging:** Regular cross-sectional imaging (PET/CT or CT of chest/abdomen/pelvis) is recommended, especially for patients with nodal disease, with a frequency of every 6-12 months for the first 3 years.
**Patient Education:** Strict sun protection, monthly self-skin and self-lymph node examinations, and immediate reporting of any new or changing lesions.
**Multidisciplinary Care:** Continued coordination between dermatology, surgery, and oncology specialties.
complications: **Disease-Related:**
High rate of local recurrence (~30%) and regional nodal recurrence (~50%).
Distant metastasis to sites including distant skin/nodes, liver, lung, bone, and brain.
Spinal cord compression from vertebral metastases.
Paraneoplastic syndromes (rare), such as Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome.
**Treatment-Related:**
**Surgery:** Lymphedema following lymph node dissection, nerve damage, scarring.
**Radiation Therapy:** Acute radiation dermatitis, mucositis; chronic fibrosis, telangiectasias, and risk of secondary malignancy.
**Immunotherapy:** Immune-related adverse events (irAEs) affecting any organ system, including colitis, hepatitis, pneumonitis, dermatitis, and endocrinopathies (e.g., thyroiditis, hypophysitis).
